html:
Nionwentsïo, meaning our beautiful land, is the territory claimed by the Huron-Wendat Nation of Wendake, near Quebec City. It covers a wide stretch of the St. Lawrence valley and the hills north of it, where Wendat families hunted and fished after the 1650s.

In 1492 the Wendat lived far to the west, in some twenty towns of longhouses between Lake Simcoe and Georgian Bay in today's Ontario, a confederacy of four or five nations that grew maize, beans and squash. The St. Lawrence valley itself was then home to the St. Lawrence Iroquoians, whom Jacques Cartier met in 1535 and who had vanished by 1600.

The Wendat were the main trading partners of New France and hosted Jesuit missions such as Sainte-Marie. Epidemics in the 1630s killed about half of them, and in 1649 the Haudenosaunee destroyed their towns in the Beaver Wars. Some survivors fled to Quebec and settled for good at Wendake in 1697. Others joined the Petun and moved west, becoming the Wyandot. In 1990 the Supreme Court of Canada upheld a 1760 British treaty with the Wendat in R. v. Sioui. See also Huron.
